nodes.title: Spl: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Spl. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A Splunk SOC analyst pulls a search returning many duplicate events that share the same `src_ip` + `dest_port`. They want ONE event PER unique (src_ip, dest_port) pair (keep the first). Which SPL command does this?
flashcards.back: The `dedup` command removes duplicate events that share the same value for a specified field. For example, `dedup src_ip` keeps only the first event for each unique source IP. You can use `dedup N fieldname` to keep the first N events per unique value.

flashcards.front: A Splunk admin counts events per host with `index=main | stats count by host`. What does this exact pipeline return?
flashcards.back: The `stats count by host` command is a transforming command that returns a table with each unique value of `host` and the count of events that have that value. The `by` clause specifies the field(s) to group by.

flashcards.front: A Splunk SPL search must match events where `status` is 404 OR 500 (both are valid HTTP error codes the SOC is investigating). Which forms are valid SPL syntax?
flashcards.back: All three syntaxes are valid in Splunk SPL. The `IN` operator (introduced in Splunk 6.3) is a shorthand for multiple OR conditions on the same field. `status IN (404, 500)` is equivalent to `status=404 OR status=500` and also to `status=(404 OR 500)`.

flashcards.front: After a search, an analyst wants the result column `src_ip` to display as `SourceIP` (purely a rename of the result column, no data change). Which SPL command?
flashcards.back: The `rename` command renames a field. `rename src_ip AS SourceIP` (the AS keyword is case-insensitive) renames the field in the results. Note that after renaming, you must use the new name in subsequent pipeline commands. The `eval` + `fields` approach also works but is less clean.

nodes.title: Knowledge Objects: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Knowledge Objects. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: An admin wants `clientip` to be queryable as ANOTHER name (e.g. `src_ip`) so legacy dashboards using `src_ip` continue to work without changing the data. Splunk supports defining `src_ip → clientip` as a search-time mapping. Both names refer to the same underlying field. Which Splunk knowledge object is this?
flashcards.back: A field alias creates an alternative name for an existing field. Both the original and alias names can be used interchangeably in searches. Field aliases are configured in Settings > Fields > Field Aliases and are applied per source type. They are useful for normalizing field names across different data sources (e.g., aliasing `src` to `src_ip` across various source types).

flashcards.front: A SOC wants to CATEGORISE events at search time without modifying the raw data. They define a SEARCH expression (e.g. `index=fw action=blocked` → category 'firewall_deny'). Any event matching the search inherits the category tag. Which Splunk knowledge object?
flashcards.back: An event type is a search expression saved as a knowledge object that categorizes events based on field-value pairs or search terms. Events matching an event type get an `eventtype` field with the event type's name. Tags can then be applied to event types. Event types are useful for grouping similar events across data sources.

flashcards.front: Splunk has two related knowledge objects. (A) TAGS — apply to specific field=value pairs (e.g., `host=web01` gets tag `production`). (B) EVENT TYPES — defined by a SEARCH expression; events matching the search inherit the event-type label. Tags can be APPLIED to event types as well. Which describes tags vs event types?
flashcards.back: A tag is a label applied to a specific field=value pair (e.g., tag the value 'sshd' in the 'process' field as 'authentication'). Tags are searched using `tag=<tagname>`. An event type is a categorization saved as a search — events matching the search get tagged with the event type name. Both help normalize and categorize data, and work well together. Tags are searched with tag=<value>

flashcards.front: A reusable SPL fragment `failed_logins` takes ONE argument (the index name). When called as `\`failed_logins(security)\``, it should expand to `index=security action=failure`. Splunk's macro syntax uses `$arg$` for argument substitution inside the macro definition. Which definition?
flashcards.back: Splunk search macros use `$argument_name$` syntax for arguments. The macro definition would contain `index=$index$ action=failure`, and you'd set the argument count to 1. The macro is invoked with backtick syntax: `` `failed_logins(main)` `` which expands to `index=main action=failure`. Argument names must match between the definition and the invocation.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.
